opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about it as a spectrum. Almost everything we do to models today is shaping from the outside. You pick training data, write a reward signal, run RLHF, write a system prompt, and hope the network internalizes what you meant. It's a bit like training a dog. You reward behaviors you like, and you don't actually know what changed inside. Usually it works well enough, but you get surprises: sycophancy, reward hacking, weird generalizations you never asked for. That's because you're working through a very narrow channel, which is the loss function, and the model is free to satisfy it in whatever way is easiest.

Direct editing is the other end. If you can open the model, find the internal representations that correspond to a concept or behavior, and intervene on them, you're no longer guessing. You can say: here's the feature for this kind of deception, or this piece of knowledge, and here's what happens when we turn it up, turn it down, or remove it. That's much closer to how we engineer every other system we depend on. Nobody builds a bridge by rewarding it when it doesn't fall down. You understand the mechanics and design accordingly.

I don't think it's either/or, though. Training will stay the main way we give models capabilities. It's incredibly powerful and editing won't replace it. But interpretability makes shaping much more precise. You can use it to audit what training actually did, catch problems before deployment, and make targeted fixes without retraining the whole model and risking regressions elsewhere. Over time I expect the two to merge: you train, look inside, edit, and you can even use what you learn from the internals to design better training signals.

The bigger point is that we're building some of the most important technology in history, and right now we mostly treat it as a black box. Moving from purely shaping behavior to actually understanding and editing the internals is what turns this from alchemy into engineering. That's the shift I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: The response compares shaping to training a dog, but does not mention a bonsai tree or selectively pruning unwanted branches.

r002.rationale: The response describes shaping and direct editing, but does not say it remains unresolved which method is most effective for changing model behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, shaping behavior and directly editing a network are really two ends of the same spectrum, and the interesting question is how much you understand about what's inside.

Shaping, which is what most of us do today through training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, is indirect. You specify what you want through data or a reward signal, and gradient descent finds some set of weights that produces that behavior. You get the outcome, but you don't really know how it got there. The model might have learned the thing you wanted, or it might have learned a shortcut that looks the same on your evaluation set and diverges somewhere you didn't test. That's the classic problem: you're steering from the outside, and the internals are opaque.

Direct editing is the other end. If you can locate the circuit or the feature that's responsible for a behavior, you can intervene on it surgically. Change this direction in activation space, clamp this feature, and the model stops doing the thing. The appeal is precision and transparency. You know exactly what you changed, and in principle you can predict the side effects, because you can see what else that component connects to.

The reality is that we're somewhere in the middle. Interpretability has gotten good enough that we can find features that correspond to meaningful concepts, and steering on them works surprisingly well for some behaviors. But most interesting behaviors aren't localized to one clean component. They're distributed, they interact, and the moment you edit one thing you discover it was load-bearing for three other things you didn't anticipate. So editing today often ends up being a diagnostic tool rather than the final intervention. You use it to understand what the model is doing, and then you go back and shape through training with much better intuition about what you're actually targeting.

The thing I find exciting is the feedback loop between the two. Training gives you capable models whose internals you can then study. Studying the internals tells you where training went wrong, where the model learned something superficial. And that in turn tells you how to change the training. Over time I think the distinction blurs, because the ideal is training that's informed by what you can see inside, and editing that's validated by how the model behaves across a wide distribution. Neither one alone gets you a model you can trust.

r002.rationale: It describes tradeoffs and a feedback loop between training and editing, but does not state that which method is most effective remains unresolved.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as two different levels of intervention. When you train a network, you’re shaping its behavior through examples and feedback. You’re saying, “Do more of this, less of that,” and letting the learning process figure out what internal changes produce that result. When you directly edit it, you’re trying to identify something inside the network and change it more precisely.

The interesting question is whether that precision is real. A change can look very targeted on a few examples but have consequences elsewhere, because the network’s representations aren’t necessarily neatly separated. And conversely, a behavioral intervention can sometimes produce a surprisingly specific change.

So I see them as complementary. Understanding the internals could help us make better interventions, but we still need to test what the network actually does afterward. Being able to edit something doesn’t automatically mean we understand it.

r002.rationale: It questions whether direct edits are truly precise and calls the methods complementary, but does not clearly state that which method is most effective remains unresolved.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as two ways of working on the same system, but at different levels. When you train a network, you’re specifying the behavior you want through examples or rewards, and letting optimization figure out how to implement it. When you edit it directly, you’re making a more specific hypothesis: this part of the network is responsible for something, and changing it will have a predictable effect.

The challenge is that a change that looks local to us might not be local to the model. You might successfully change one answer while affecting other behaviors you didn’t test. But you can have a similar problem with training: getting the behavior you want on your examples doesn’t necessarily mean the model learned the underlying rule you intended.

So I see these approaches as complementary. Understanding the internals can help us make more precise interventions, and behavioral testing tells us whether those interventions actually did what we hoped.
